claims.text: Corrosion resistance in steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by formation of a stable protective oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer is enriched with chromium and nickel.
The protective oxide layer inhibits further oxidation and chemical attack.
Chromium in the steel promotes formation of a dense, adherent oxide layer.
Nickel in the steel promotes formation of a dense, adherent oxide layer.
The dense, adherent oxide layer prevents ingress of corrosive agents.
Preventing ingress of corrosive agents reduces further corrosion.
Steels with higher chromium and nickel contents will have significantly lower corrosion rates than steels with lower or no chromium and nickel under identical conditions.
The proposed relationship should hold over chromium and nickel concentrations typically used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power steels.
The proposed relationship should hold under operating conditions relevant to chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
Threshold chromium and nickel concentrations for optimal corrosion resistance may depend on the corrosive environment.
The controlled study will vary chromium and nickel contents while holding the corrosive exposure conditions identical.
Corrosion rate will be measured over time by weight loss or electrochemical techniques.
Oxide-layer composition and thickness will be characterized using X-ray diffraction or electron microscopy.
Failure of higher-chromium and higher-nickel steels to show lower corrosion rates or a stable protective oxide layer relative to baseline steels would falsify the hypothesis.
